01  /  Overview

Same store, four different customers.

Every retailer already knows this intuitively — the person buying a $30 lipstick and the person buying a $1,200 laptop are not the same customer, even if they walk through the same door. This project turns that intuition into a statistically grounded, repeatable model.

The business problem: a retailer has 1,000 transactions and no formal way to tell which customers matter most, what they buy, or how to talk to them. Marketing spend, loyalty perks, and email campaigns are all being sent the same way to everyone.

The goal of this analysis is to segment customers into distinct, interpretable groups using unsupervised machine learning — no labels, no surveys, just transaction data — and turn each group into a persona the business can actually act on.

The end result, previewed below: 21.5% of customers generate 64.4% of revenue. That single number is the difference between a blanket marketing strategy and a targeted one.

04  /  Feature Scaling & PCA

Putting every feature on the same footing.

Age ranges from 18–70. Total Amount ranges from $25 to $2,000. Left unscaled, K-Means would treat spend as almost 30× more "important" than age purely because of its bigger numbers — not because it actually matters more.

Why scale: K-Means clusters points by Euclidean distance. Any feature with a larger numeric range will silently dominate that distance calculation. StandardScaler fixes this by transforming every numeric feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so Age, Quantity, Price per Unit, and Total Amount all get an equal vote.

Why PCA: after scaling, the data still lives in a multi-dimensional space that's impossible to plot directly. Principal Component Analysis rotates the data onto new axes — "principal components" — ranked by how much variance (information) each one captures, so the segments can be visualized in 2D and 3D without losing the story.

Result — the first two principal components capture 60.1% of total variance; the first three capture 79.8%. That's enough signal to trust a 2D/3D plot as a genuine picture of the cluster structure, not a distortion of it.
Fig. 1 — Explained variance by principal componentscikit-learn PCA

PC1 is essentially a "spend axis" — driven almost entirely by Total Amount and Price per Unit. This is why the four clusters visually separate left-to-right in the PCA scatter plot below: it's the price tier of what people buy, more than anything else, that defines the segments.

05  /  Choosing K

How many segments actually exist?

K-Means needs to be told how many clusters (K) to find — it won't discover that number on its own. Two diagnostics were used together to choose it.

Fig. 2 — Inertia (elbow) vs. silhouette score, K=2 to 10scikit-learn KMeans

The elbow method plots inertia (how tightly packed each cluster is) against K. Inertia always drops as K increases, so the goal is to find the "elbow" — the point where adding more clusters stops buying much improvement. Here that bend sits around K=4–5.

The silhouette score measures how well separated the clusters are (−1 to 1, higher is better). It's technically highest at K=2 (0.316), but two clusters would only split customers into a vague "big spenders vs. everyone else" — not useful for targeting.

Decision — K=4 was selected: it sits right at the elbow, keeps a reasonable silhouette score (0.252), and — most importantly — produces four segments that map cleanly onto real business personas rather than statistically-optimal but meaningless splits.

Revenue Index = % of revenue ÷ % of customers. A value above 1 means the segment over-indexes on revenue relative to its size; below 1 means it under-indexes.

The headline insight — Cluster 3 is only 21.5% of the customer base but drives 64.4% of total revenue. Cluster 0, by contrast, is the largest group (31.5%) but contributes just 3.6%. This is a textbook Pareto pattern, and it's the single most actionable finding in the whole analysis.

08  /  Personas

Four customers, four price tags.

Turning the numbers above into personas the marketing and merchandising teams can actually use.

The largest group by headcount, but the lowest value. They buy a single low-priced item ($35 avg unit price) and don't come back often within this window. This is the everyday, price-sensitive browser.

StrategyLow-cost automated nurture (email/SMS), entry-level bundles, and low-friction loyalty points to lift purchase frequency without discounting margin away.

Premium Occasional

Buys just one or two items per visit — but they're expensive ($411 avg unit price). Think a single electronics purchase. High value, low frequency: the classic "big ticket" shopper.

StrategyExtended warranties, financing/installment options, and post-purchase cross-sell timed around typical replacement cycles for big-ticket items.

The opposite pattern from C1: buys more units (3.6 avg) of cheaper goods. Basket-builders rather than big spenders — comfortable with volume, price-conscious per item.

Strategy"Buy more, save more" tiered volume discounts and multi-buy promotions — this segment is already primed to add items to the basket.

Buys a lot (3.5 avg units) of expensive items ($392 avg unit price). Only a fifth of the customer base but nearly two-thirds of all revenue — this segment is the business, financially speaking.

StrategyWhite-glove retention: dedicated account support, early access to new inventory, and VIP-tier perks. Losing one C3 customer costs as much revenue as losing ~26 C0 customers.
09  /  Business Recommendations

What the business should actually do with this.

Turning the segmentation into concrete next steps for marketing, retention, and merchandising.

01

Protect revenue concentration risk

With 64.4% of revenue sitting in 21.5% of customers, build a dedicated retention program for C3 — churn monitoring, proactive outreach, and loyalty tiers that reward continued spend rather than one-off discounts.

02

Convert C1's occasional visits into recurring ones

C1 already spends well per visit ($604 avg) but rarely returns. Targeted win-back campaigns timed to typical replacement cycles for big-ticket goods could meaningfully lift visit frequency.

03

Grow basket size within C2

C2 already buys in volume — tiered "spend $X more, save Y%" thresholds and bundling nudge this segment toward higher-value baskets without needing to acquire a single new customer.

04

Don't over-invest in C0

C0 is the largest group by headcount but the smallest by revenue. Keep engagement here low-cost and automated; heavy discounting to this segment would erode margin for minimal incremental revenue.

10  /  Limitations & Future Work

Where this model should be pushed further.

A fair segmentation report is honest about its own edges. Three things would meaningfully strengthen this analysis in a v2.

Note on Transaction ID — the notebook's numeric feature selection (select_dtypes(include='number')) unintentionally included Transaction ID as a clustering feature. Since IDs are just row order, this adds noise rather than signal — visible in its unusually high PC2 loading (0.682) alongside Age. Re-running the pipeline with identifier columns explicitly excluded is the highest-priority fix for a v2 of this model.
Modest silhouette score — at 0.252, clusters are meaningfully separated but do overlap, which is expected and honest for real retail behavior data rather than synthetic, clearly separable clusters. Business interpretability was intentionally prioritized over squeezing out a marginally higher statistical score.
Single time snapshot — the dataset has no repeat-purchase or recency signal per customer. A genuine RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) feature set — plus testing hierarchical or DBSCAN clustering as a cross-check against K-Means — would be the natural next iteration of this project.
